to strive, to threaten, to profess; it is an old epic verb, of which Homer used only the third person singular στεῦται and στεῦτο, noted by Hesychius, στεῦτο: he stood in thought and determined, he affirmed: an example of the first person στεῦμαι is in Orph. Lith. 82 στεῦμαι – δείξειν, if Hermann correctly conjectured this for ὑπισχνοῦμαι

Among the tragedians there is one example of this verb, where it should be noted that στεῦται [he strives] is used in the singular for the plural στεῦνται [they strive], about which the scholiast says: "κλῦθ᾽, Ἀλαλά, Πολέμου θύγατερ, ᾷ θύεται ἄνδρες [Hear, Alala, daughter of War, to whom men are sacrificed]" in a dithyramb (of Pindar, as it seems). Thus στεῦται [he strives] is singular instead of plural.
The neighbors of sacred Tmolus strive (M has στεῦνται, but with the ν expunged) to cast the yoke of slavery upon Hellas
